Every module goes the same way, so you always know where you are.
First the idea, as a picture. Each module has one mental model, and once you can see it, the questions mostly answer themselves.
Then the questions, in the order the page has them, with the page's question numbers. When a question was asked often in real interviews, I'll tell you how often.
For the questions that come up the most, you get a model answer, written so you can say it out loud in about thirty seconds.
And each module ends with a check. When the timer ring appears, pause if you need to, and answer out loud before I do. Recalling an answer yourself is what moves it from the screen into your memory.
One thing before we start: where the counts come from. They come from four hundred and fifty six real interview write-ups that mention Python.
Decorators lead, with seventeen. That's module three.
Generators and yield, sixteen. Module four.
Threads versus processes versus asyncio, thirteen. Module seven.
Comprehensions, eleven. Module two.
Memory and garbage collection, ten. Module eight.
So those five get the most time. Everything else still gets explained properly, because a follow-up question can land anywhere.
Module one. Python basics and the data model. This is the module that explains most Python surprises, and it rests on a single idea: names point to objects.

Here is the idea the whole module hangs on. In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It's a name, a label, tied to an object that lives somewhere in memory. A equals the list one, two makes a list object, and then ties the name a to it.
Now b equals a. Nothing is copied. Python just ties a second label, b, to the very same object. There is still one list.
So when you call b dot append three, you change that one object, and a sees the change, because a points at the same thing.

But b equals a new list, nine, is different. That doesn't change any object. It moves the label b to a new object. Changing an object, and moving a name, are the two things to keep apart for this whole module.
Question one, asked in two write-ups. How is Python different from Java?
A good answer compares a few dimensions, not a list of syntax: typing, how the code runs, memory, concurrency, and the style of the language.

On the Python side. Typing is dynamic: a type belongs to the value, not to the variable, and it's checked when the code runs. Type hints exist, but Python itself doesn't enforce them. CPython compiles your code to bytecode and interprets it, with no just-in-time compiler by default. Memory is freed by reference counting, plus a collector for cycles. The GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. And everything, even an int or a function, is an object.

On the Java side. Static typing, checked at compile time. Bytecode on the JVM, where a JIT compiles hot code to machine code, which is a big reason Java is faster for CPU-heavy loops. A tracing garbage collector. Real parallel threads. And a split between primitives and objects.

The one-line summary: Python trades raw speed for speed of writing. And when speed matters, the heavy lifting happens in C extensions like NumPy, or in other processes, which is exactly how AI code in Python stays fast.
Question two. What does everything is an object mean, and how do names and references work?
Cover three things. Every object has an identity, a type and a value. Names are references to objects. And arguments are passed by object reference.
Everything is an object means every value carries three things. An identity, which the id function shows: in CPython, it's the object's address in memory. A type, which says what it is. And a value.

And everything really means everything. A function is an object of type function. So you can give it another name, pass it to another function, or store it in a dictionary. That one fact is what makes decorators possible in module three.
Now the part interviews really test: what happens when you pass an argument. The caller has a name, nums, pointing at a list.
Calling add with nums makes the parameter, items, a new name for the same object. Nothing is copied. This is called pass by object reference, or call by sharing.
So if the function mutates the object, with items dot append four, the caller sees it, because there is only one list.

But if the function assigns, items equals a new list, it only moves its own local label. The caller's list is untouched. Mutation is visible to the caller; rebinding is not. That sentence is the whole answer.
Question three, asked in five write-ups. Which types are mutable and which are immutable, and why does it matter?
Name the types on each side, say what a change does to each, and then give the places where it matters, because that's what makes the answer sound experienced.
Immutable types can never change after they're made: the numbers, strings and bytes, tuples and frozensets, and None. When you seem to change one, Python builds a new object and moves the name.
Mutable types change in place: lists, dicts, sets, bytearrays, and most classes you write yourself. A change is visible through every name that points at the object.
And the reason it matters most: dict keys and set members must be hashable, which in practice means immutable. A tuple can be a key. A list can't.
Here's the difference in one picture. S is the string hi, and t equals s, so two names, one string.
Now s plus equals an exclamation mark. Strings can't change, so Python builds a new string, hi with the mark, and moves s to it. T still sees the old hi.
Same operator on a list. A is one, two, and b equals a.
A plus equals a list with three. Lists are mutable, so plus equals extends the list in place, and b sees one, two, three. Same symbol, different behaviour, and the difference is mutability.
A favourite follow-up. True or false: a tuple is immutable, so nothing inside it can ever change.
False. The tuple holds references, and those can't change. But if one of them points at a list, that list can still change.
So a tuple holding a list, then appending to the list, works fine, and the tuple now shows the new item. And because its contents can change, that tuple can't be hashed, so it can't be a dict key.
Here's how I'd say it in an interview.
Names in Python are references to objects, and assignment never copies.
Immutable objects, like ints, strings and tuples, can't change. Anything that looks like a change builds a new object.
Mutable objects, like lists, dicts and sets, change in place, and every name pointing at them sees the change.
It matters when you pass arguments, for default arguments, and for any state shared between parts of a program.
And only hashable values, which in practice means immutable ones, can be dictionary keys or set members.
Question four. What is the difference between is, and double equals?
Value versus identity, and the one rule for when to use is.

Double equals compares values. It calls the dunder eq method. Is compares identity: are these two names pointing at the very same object? Here a and b are two separate lists that happen to hold the same values. So a double equals b is true, but a is b is false.
C equals a ties c to a's object, so c is a is true. Equal value is double equals. Same object is is.
The trap that comes with it. X equals two fifty six, y equals two fifty six, and x is y is true. So is works for numbers, right?
No. That's an accident. CPython keeps a single cached copy of small integers, from minus five to two fifty six, and of some strings. With bigger numbers, the same test can be false.
So the rule: use is only for singletons. None, True, False, and sentinel objects you create yourself. If x is None, yes. If x is five, never.
Question five, asked in three write-ups. What's the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
Three things to separate: plain assignment, a shallow copy, and a deep copy, and what each one shares.
Take a grid, a list of two lists. Plain assignment, same equals grid, copies nothing at all. One outer list, two names.
A shallow copy, with dot copy, or a slice, or list of grid, makes a new outer list. But its elements are the same row objects. So changing shallow's row zero, changes grid's row zero too.
A deep copy, with copy dot deepcopy, copies recursively, all the way down, so nothing is shared. Shallow copies the container. Deep copies everything inside it.

The same idea hides in a classic trap. A list containing zero times three, then times three. The outer times three repeats the reference, not the row, so you get three references to one row. Set one cell, and it shows up in every row.
The fix is a comprehension, which runs the inner expression again for each row, so every row is its own list.
Question six. What is the mutable default argument problem?
Say when default values are created, show what goes wrong, and give the standard fix.
Default values are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function object. Not on every call.

So a mutable default, like an empty list, is shared by every call that doesn't pass its own. The second call sees the first call's item. You can even see the shared list, in add item dot dunder defaults.
The fix: default to None, and create the new list inside the body. The same once-only rule bites with things like a default of datetime dot now: the time is frozen at definition.
Question seven. How does Python execute code? CPython, bytecode, and the Python virtual machine.
Walk the pipeline from source code to running bytecode, and say where the speed goes.
CPython is the standard interpreter, written in C. It starts from your source file.
First it breaks the text into tokens and parses them into an abstract syntax tree.

Then it compiles that tree to bytecode: simple instructions for a stack-based machine. For imported modules, the bytecode is cached in the pycache folder, as dot pyc files, so the next import skips this step.
Then the Python virtual machine, which is really a big evaluation loop written in C, executes those instructions one at a time. You can see them yourself with the dis module.

And this is where the speed goes. There's no just-in-time compiler by default, and every single operation checks types while the program runs. That's why a pure Python loop is slow, and why PyPy, which has a JIT, or C extensions like NumPy, are much faster.

Check 1. A is a list holding the list one and the list two. B equals a dot copy. Then b, index zero, dot append nine. What is a now? A, unchanged, copy made it independent. B, the first inner list becomes one, nine. C, nine gets added at the end. Or D, a type error.
B. A becomes the list one nine, and two. Copy is shallow. It made a new outer list, but b's first element is the same inner list as a's first element, so appending to it shows through both.
Check 2. Why does a function with the default, when equals datetime dot now, print the same time on every call?

Because default values are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, not on every call. So the time is frozen at the moment the function was defined. Default to None, and compute the time inside the body.
Module two. The built-in data structures: lists, tuples, dicts, sets and strings, how they work inside, and the comprehensions that build them. Eleven write-ups asked about comprehensions alone.
Here's the module in one picture. A list is ordered and mutable, and inside it's a growable array of pointers. So getting item i is instant, but searching means walking the list.
A tuple is the same kind of array, but fixed: it can't change, so it can be hashed, as long as what's inside can.
A dict maps keys to values, and inside it's a hash table, so looking a key up is constant time on average.
And a set is a hash table with keys and no values. So asking: is this item in the set, is constant time too.
So there are really only two machines inside. Arrays answer: what's at position i. Hash tables answer: is this key here. Most questions in this module are one of those two.
Question eight, asked in five write-ups. What's the difference between a list and a tuple?
Mutability first, then what follows from it: hashability, memory, and what each one is used to mean.
A list is mutable. You append, remove and sort it in place. Because it can change, it isn't hashable, so it can't be a dict key. And it keeps spare room so it can grow.

A tuple is immutable. Once made, it's fixed. So if its items are hashable, the tuple is too, and it can be a key, like a pair of coordinates. It's smaller, and a little faster to create. And it usually means a record: fixed positions, each with its own meaning, like latitude and longitude.
And one detail interviewers like: it's the comma that makes a tuple, not the brackets. One, comma, in brackets, is a tuple. One in brackets is just the number one.
Said in an interview.
A list is mutable, a tuple is immutable.
Because of that, a tuple of hashable items is itself hashable, so it can be a dictionary key or a set member. A list never can.
Tuples are smaller and slightly faster. Lists over-allocate memory so they can grow.
So I use a list for a collection that changes, and a tuple for a fixed record, like a coordinate or a row returned from a database.
Question nine. How is a list implemented, and what are the time complexities?
Describe the dynamic array, explain why append is cheap, and then say which operations are slow.
A Python list is a dynamic array, and what it stores are pointers to objects, not the objects themselves. That's why one list can hold an int, a string and None side by side.
Indexing is instant: Python computes where slot two is, and goes straight there. Constant time.

When the block is full and you append, CPython allocates a bigger block, copies the pointers across, and leaves spare room. It grows by about an eighth plus a little, which is a smaller step than Java's.
So most appends just fill the next spare slot. The occasional copy is spread across many appends, which is what amortised constant time means.

But inserting at the front, or popping from the front, has to move every pointer one slot. That's linear time. So if you need a queue, use collections dot deque, which adds and removes at both ends in constant time.
So, the costs. Indexing, length, append, and pop from the end: constant time.
Insert at the front, pop from the front, and remove a value: linear, because things shift.
Searching, with in or dot index, is linear too, because the list has to look at each item. If you test membership a lot, use a set.
And sorting is n log n, using Timsort, which is stable.
Question ten. How does a dict work internally?
The hash table, step by step: hashing to a slot, collisions, why keys must be immutable, and why dicts keep insertion order.
A dict is a hash table. To store alice, Python calls hash on the key, takes it modulo the table size, and that picks a slot. Alice lands in slot five.
Bob hashes to slot two.
Carol hashes to slot five, but that's taken. That's a collision. CPython uses open addressing: it probes other slots in a fixed pseudo-random order until it finds a free one. Carol lands in seven.
And a lookup repeats the same steps. Hash the key, go to the slot, and confirm it's the right key with double equals. No scanning. That's why lookup is constant time on average.

Four things follow from that picture. First, keys must be hashable, and the hash must never change. If a key could change after being stored, it would sit in the wrong slot forever and never be found. That's why lists can't be keys.
Second, two keys that are equal must have the same hash. So if you override dunder eq in your own class, you must override dunder hash as well.
Third, the table grows when it's about two thirds full, to keep probe chains short. With lots of collisions, the worst case is linear, but that's rare.

And fourth, dicts keep insertion order, guaranteed since Python three point seven. Inside, there's a small index array of slots, pointing into a dense array of entries kept in the order you added them.
Question eleven. What is a set, and when do you use it?
It's the same hash table without values, so say what that makes fast.

A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items. It's a hash table with keys and no values. So the big use is fast membership: is this user in seen? That's a hash lookup, not a scan. It's how you deduplicate, and how BFS tracks visited nodes. And note: empty curly braces make an empty dict. An empty set is set with brackets.
Sets also do algebra. Union with the bar, intersection with the ampersand, and difference with minus. Common followers, missing ids, that kind of question.
And frozenset is the immutable version, so it's hashable, and can itself be a dict key or sit inside another set.
Question twelve, asked twice. Why are strings immutable, and how should you build strings efficiently?
What immutability buys you, and the consequence for building strings.

Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode characters. That buys a lot: they're hashable, so they can be dict keys. They're safe to share between threads and functions. And CPython can intern and cache them. The cost: every change makes a new string. So adding to a string in a loop can copy everything built so far, every time, which is quadratic. CPython sometimes optimises this case, but you can't rely on it.
The fix is the idiom interviewers want to hear: collect the pieces in a list, and join them once at the end. That's linear.
Question thirteen. How does slicing work?
The three parts of a slice, negative indexes, and two facts that surprise people.
A slice has a start, a stop, and a step. Indexes count from zero on the left, and negative indexes count from the right, so minus one is the last item.
S from one to four gives Y, T, H. Start is included, stop is excluded, so you get index one, two and three.
Leave out the stop, and it runs to the end. S from minus three is the last three: H, O, N.
A step of two takes every second item: P, T, O.
And a step of minus one walks backwards, so s with colon colon minus one is the classic way to reverse a sequence.
Two facts that surprise people. Slicing a list creates a new list, a shallow copy. So lst with colon is a quick copy.
And slices never raise an index error. Slicing past the end just gives you an empty list, while indexing past the end raises.
Question fourteen, asked in eleven write-ups. What are list, dict and set comprehensions, and generator expressions?
Show the shape of each, then the one difference that matters: building everything now, or one item at a time.
A comprehension builds a new collection from an iterable in one expression. Read it as: the expression, for each item, if the condition holds. This list comprehension squares the even numbers.
Change the brackets to curly braces, and you get a set. Add a key and a colon, and you get a dict.
Use round brackets, and you get a generator expression. It doesn't build anything. It produces items one at a time, on demand, so passing it straight to sum, any, max or join uses almost no memory.
Two for clauses nest, and they read in the same order as nested loops: the outer one first.

It replaces exactly this loop: an empty list, a for, an if, and an append. The comprehension is shorter, and a little faster, because the append happens inside the interpreter, without a method lookup each time.
Here's why the brackets matter. Ten million squares, summed.
With square brackets, Python builds the whole list of ten million squares first, which is hundreds of megabytes, and only then sums them.
With round brackets, sum pulls one square at a time, adds it, and throws it away. Memory stays flat.

Same answer. So use a generator expression when you'll pass over the items once. Use a list when you need them again, or need their length, or need to index into them. And keep comprehensions simple: if it needs two conditions and a nested loop, write the loop.
The answer, out loud.
A comprehension builds a list, a dict or a set from an iterable in one expression, with an optional filter.
It's more readable than an append loop, and a little faster.
A generator expression, written with round brackets, produces items lazily, one at a time, so it uses constant memory.
I use it whenever the result is consumed once, like passing it to sum, any or join.
And if the logic needs several steps, or has side effects, I write a normal loop instead. Readability wins.
Question fifteen. What does the collections module give you?
Five containers, each with the problem it's built for.
Counter counts things. Hand it a list of words, and most common three gives you the top three. Word-frequency questions, in one line.
Defaultdict gives a missing key a default value, from a function you pass in, like list. So grouping is just: groups of k, dot append. No checking whether the key exists.
Deque, a double-ended queue, adds and removes at both ends in constant time. It's the queue for breadth-first search, and for sliding windows.
OrderedDict keeps an order you can change, with move to end, and pop item from either end. That's the classic way to build an LRU cache, which comes back in module eleven.
And namedtuple is a tuple whose fields have names, so p dot x instead of p of zero. Interviews love these five. Counter, defaultdict and deque especially.
Question sixteen. How do sorting, the key argument, enumerate and zip work?
The difference between sorted and sort, what key does, why stability matters, and the two looping helpers.
Dot sort sorts a list in place and returns None. A classic bug is writing x equals x dot sort. Sorted works on any iterable and returns a new list.

The key argument is a function computed once per element, and Python sorts by its result. To sort by several things, return a tuple. And to flip one part, negate it: minus points, then name, gives highest points first, with ties in name order. Python's sort is Timsort: n log n, fast on data that's partly sorted, and stable, so equal keys keep their original order.
And the two looping helpers. Enumerate gives you the index and the value together, so you never write range of len. Zip walks two or more iterables in step, and stops at the shortest.
Check 3. Why is checking whether a key is in a dict constant time, but checking whether it's in a list linear?
Because a dict is a hash table. It hashes the key, jumps straight to the slot, and compares one entry. A list only knows positions, not values, so finding a value means comparing items one by one.

Check 4. You need the total length of fifty million lines from a file. Square brackets or round brackets inside sum? A, square brackets, lists are faster. B, round brackets, one line in memory at a time. C, either, Python optimises it. Or D, neither, use a for loop.
B. Round brackets. The generator expression hands one line's length at a time to sum, so memory stays flat. Square brackets would build a list of fifty million lengths before adding any of them.
Module three. Functions and scope. This module holds the single most asked Python topic, decorators, and the way to understand decorators is to build them from three simpler facts first.
Here's the idea behind this whole module. Three facts about functions.
One. A function is an object, as we saw in module one. You can pass it to another function, return it, or store it.
Two. You can define a function inside another function. Every time the outer one runs, a brand new inner function is made.
Three. The inner function remembers the variables of the outer one, even after the outer function has returned. That's called a closure.
Put the three together: a function that takes a function, defines a wrapper inside, and returns it. That's a decorator. Keep these three facts in mind, and the rest of the module follows.
Question seventeen, asked in three write-ups. What are star args and double star kwargs?
Two jobs to explain: collecting extra arguments in a definition, and unpacking them in a call. Then the parameter order.

In a function definition, star args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple, and double star kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dict. The names args and kwargs are only a convention. The stars do the work.

In a call, the stars do the opposite. They unpack. Star nums spreads a list into positional arguments, and double star opts spreads a dict into keyword arguments. This is how a wrapper passes everything through to the function it wraps.

And the order of parameters: positional-only ones before a slash, then normal ones, then star args, then keyword-only ones, then double star kwargs. A bare star means: everything after me must be passed by name, like timeout here. That's a nice way to make calls readable.
Question eighteen. What is the LEGB rule, and what do global and nonlocal do?
The lookup order, the rule that assignment makes a name local, and the two keywords that change that.
When you use a name, Python looks it up through nested scopes. Here, a function inner, defined inside a function outer, in a module.
First, the local scope: the function that's running. X is found right there.
If it's not local, Python tries the enclosing scopes: the functions around this one. Total lives in outer.
Then the global scope, which means the module's top level. That's where model is.
And last, the built-ins, like len and print.
If the name isn't in any of them, you get a name error. Local, enclosing, global, built-in: L, E, G, B.

The rule that trips people up: if a function assigns to a name anywhere, that name is local for the whole function. So count plus equals one fails with an unbound local error, because Python decided count is local, and it has no value yet.
The global keyword says: this name means the module's variable. It works, but global state is usually a smell.

And nonlocal says: this name means the variable in the enclosing function. That's how an inner function changes state it closed over, like this counter. Global reaches the module. Nonlocal reaches the function around you.
Question nineteen. What is a closure, and what is the late-binding gotcha?
What a closure remembers, and the consequence: it captures variables, not values.

A closure is an inner function that remembers variables from the enclosing scope, even after that scope has finished. Make counter has returned, but the step function it returned still holds on to n. Python keeps n in a small object called a cell, and you can see it in the function's dunder closure.
Call c1 twice, and n is two. The state lives in the closure, with no class needed.
Call make counter again, and you get a new function, with its own n. Each closure has its own private state. That's what decorators use to remember the function they wrap.

Now the gotcha. Make three lambdas in a loop, each returning i, and call them. You get two, two, two. All three closures share the one variable i, and they read it only when they're called, after the loop has finished with i equal to two. Closures capture variables, not values.
The classic fix is a default argument: lambda i equals i. Default values are evaluated when the function is defined, so each lambda freezes its own i.
Or bind the value explicitly with functools dot partial. Same idea: capture the value now, not the variable later.
Question twenty. The most asked Python question in the whole data set: seventeen write-ups. What are decorators, and how do they work?
Give the definition, show what the at sign really does, write one, and mention functools dot wraps. Usually you'll be asked to write one on the spot.
A decorator is a function that takes a function, and returns a new function, usually a wrapper that adds behaviour before or after the original. Timed takes func.

Inside, it defines a wrapper. Star args and double star kwargs let the wrapper accept any arguments and pass them all through. It starts a timer, calls the original, prints how long it took, and returns the original's result.
And it returns the wrapper. Not calls it. Returns it.
Then the at sign. At timed, above def answer, is just shorthand for: answer equals timed of answer. That's all the syntax does. The name answer now points at the wrapper.
Here's what happens to the name. After def, answer points at the original function.
After the decorator runs, the name answer points at the wrapper. The original isn't gone. It lives on inside the wrapper's closure, as func. So every call goes through the wrapper first.

And that's why functools dot wraps matters. Without it, the wrapper's name would be wrapper, its docstring would be lost, and logs, debuggers and frameworks like FastAPI that read the signature would see the wrong thing. Wraps copies the name and docstring across, and keeps the original reachable as dunder wrapped.
Decorators stack. With at log on top of at timed, the one nearest the def wraps first. Answer equals log of timed of answer.
Timed sits inside, closest to the function.
Log wraps around everything, so it's the outermost layer.
So a call goes in through log first, then timed, then the function, and the result comes back out the other way. Top runs first on the way in, last on the way out. It's an onion.
Here's the answer to say out loud.
A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, usually a wrapper around it.
The at syntax above a def is just shorthand for: f equals decorator of f.
It works because functions are objects, and the wrapper is a closure that keeps a reference to the original.
The wrapper accepts star args and double star kwargs and passes them through, and I use functools dot wraps so the name and docstring survive.
I'd use one for logging, timing, retries, caching or auth checks: anywhere I want behaviour around a function without editing the function itself.
Question twenty one. How do you write a decorator that takes arguments?
One more level of nesting, and what at retry of three really calls.
A decorator with arguments needs one more level. The outer function takes the arguments.
It returns the real decorator, which takes the function.
Which returns the wrapper, which runs on every call. Three levels: arguments, then function, then call.
The way to see it: at repeat of three is a call. Repeat of three runs first, and returns a decorator. Then that decorator is applied to ping. So it's ping equals repeat of three, of ping.
Question twenty two, asked in three write-ups. Write a decorator that logs every call: arguments, duration, and the result or the exception. And what happens on a recursive function?
The decorator itself, then the follow-up, which is the part that separates people.
The shape is the timer we just wrote, with a try. Start the clock, and call the function.
If it raises, log the error with the arguments, and then re-raise with a bare raise. A logging decorator must never swallow the exception: the caller still has to see it.
Otherwise, log the result and the duration, and return the result. Use repr for the arguments, so a string shows with its quotes.

Now the follow-up. Decorate a recursive function like fib. Inside fib, the name fib is looked up at call time, and it now points at the wrapper. So every recursive call goes through the wrapper, and fib of twenty logs nearly twenty two thousand lines, and the timing is nonsense.
The fix: decorate a thin outer function, and keep the recursion in an inner one that the decorator never sees. Or track the call depth inside the wrapper, and only log at depth zero.
Question twenty three. Write a retry decorator for a flaky LLM API call. Which errors do you retry, and how long do you wait?
The code is the easy part. The answer is decided by what you retry, and how you wait.
Retry only transient errors: things that might work a second later. A 429, which means rate limited. Timeouts and dropped connections. And 5 hundred errors from the provider.
Never retry permanent errors. A 400, bad request. A 401 or 403, a bad key or no access. Or a context length error.
Those fail the same way every time, so retrying them just burns money and adds latency.
How long to wait: double the wait each time. Half a second, one, two, four, and then a cap, here eight seconds, so you never wait forever.

And add random jitter to every wait. If a thousand clients failed at the same moment, jitter spreads their retries out, instead of hitting the provider again all at once. If the provider sends a Retry After header, wait exactly that long.
It's a decorator with arguments, so three levels. The arguments are how many times, the base delay, the cap, and which exception types count as transient.
The wrapper loops over attempts, and returns as soon as a call succeeds.
It catches only the listed exceptions. Anything else, like a bad request, flies straight out. And on the last attempt, it re-raises, so the caller sees the real error, never a silent None.

Otherwise it waits: the base delay doubled per attempt, capped, plus jitter. In async code, it's the same shape, with async def and await asyncio dot sleep. Never time dot sleep inside async code. And in real projects, a library like tenacity, or the SDK's own max retries, does this for you.

Module eight. Memory, modules and tooling. Memory and garbage collection was asked in ten write-ups, and it all starts from one number every object carries.
Here's the idea. Every object in CPython carries a count of how many references point at it. A equals a big dict: count one.
B equals a, and storing it in a cache: count three.
Delete a, and set b to None. The count drops to one. But the cache still holds it, so it stays alive.
Clear the cache, the count hits zero, and the object is freed at that exact moment. That's reference counting, and it's how CPython frees most memory: immediately, and predictably.
Question fifty two, asked in ten write-ups. How does memory management and garbage collection work in Python?
Reference counting, the cycle collector, how the allocator behaves, and what leaks look like in Python.

Reference counting has one blind spot: cycles. Node A points at B, and B points back at A. Your code drops its names, so nothing outside can reach them, but each still has a count of one, because of the other. They'd never be freed.

So CPython adds a cycle collector, the gc module. Every so often, it looks for groups of container objects that are only reachable from each other, and frees them. It's generational: new objects are checked often, objects that survive are checked less, because most objects die young.

Small objects are allocated from pools by Python's own allocator, pymalloc. Freed memory is reused by Python, but isn't always returned to the operating system, so a process can stay large after a spike.

Python leaks aren't lost pointers, as in C. They're references you forgot about: an unbounded cache, a global list that grows on every request, a closure holding a big object, or LRU cache on a method.
To find them, tracemalloc takes snapshots of where memory was allocated, and you compare two of them.
And to use less: generators instead of lists, dunder slots for many small objects, caches with a size limit, and dropping big objects as soon as you're done.
Put together, as an answer.
CPython uses reference counting: every object counts its references, and it's freed the moment the count reaches zero.
On top of that, a generational cycle collector frees groups of objects that only reference each other.
Small objects come from pymalloc's pools, and freed memory isn't always returned to the operating system.
In practice, leaks in Python are forgotten references: unbounded caches, growing globals, closures holding big objects.
I'd find one with tracemalloc snapshots, and fix it with bounded caches, generators, and not keeping state around longer than needed.

Question sixty three, asked in six write-ups. Implement an LRU cache.
Both get and put in constant time. The trick is combining a hash map with an order you can change in constant time.

An LRU cache, least recently used, keeps at most a fixed number of items, and when it's full, it throws out the one used longest ago. Picture the keys in order of use: oldest on the left, most recent on the right. Put a, b and c.
Get a: it's a hit, so a becomes the most recently used, and moves to the right end.
Now put d. The cache is full, so evict from the left: b, the least recently used. And d goes on the right.

To make all of this constant time, you need two things: a hash map to find any key instantly, and an order where you can move a key to the end, or drop the first one, instantly. A dict plus a doubly linked list. Or in Python, OrderedDict, which is exactly that.
In Python, the clean implementation uses OrderedDict, which keeps a hash table plus a doubly linked list of its keys.
Get: if the key is missing, return minus one. Otherwise, move it to the end, marking it most recent, and return the value.

Put: set the value, move it to the end, and if we're over capacity, pop the first item, which is the least recently used. Every step is constant time. If the interviewer says no OrderedDict, build the same thing: a dict from key to node, and a doubly linked list with dummy head and tail nodes.
